title: Credit-card cost, access, rewards, and dispute exposure differ across the US market
source_unit: US credit-card market, issuer account, cardholder credit-tier, and dispute measures

denominator.unit: national market report snapshot; measures use metric-specific account, balance, purchase-volume, or issuer universes

credit_card_balances.unit: US dollars; consumer credit-card balances exceeded $1.2 trillion

average_balance_per_cardholder.unit: US dollars per cardholder; approximate average monthly balance

interest_assessed.unit: US dollars in interest charges assessed

observations.method: CFPB 2025 Consumer Credit Card Market Report using multiple data sources as of the end of 2024, including de-identified credit records and issuer-reported data.
observations.uncertainty: Market totals and averages use different account, issuer, balance, and reporting universes. The report distinguishes interest or fees assessed from amounts necessarily paid; nominal totals are not household welfare measures.
observations.subgroup: Market-wide 2024 measures; the report separately conditions many measures on credit-score tier and product type.
observations.counterinterpretation: Higher balances and charges can reflect increased cardholding, inflation, credit demand, or account composition as well as greater household pressure; aggregate totals do not identify who ultimately bears a merchant fee.

observations.period: 2024; purchase volume, credit tier, and promotional pricing

denominator.unit: US dollars in 2024 purchase volume for CFPB Y-14+ issuer universe

purchase_volume_growth.unit: percent annual growth in credit-card spending

introductory_apr_purchase_volume.unit: US dollars in purchase volume on cards with a zero-percent introductory APR promotion

introductory_apr_balances.unit: US dollars in year-end balances on cards with an introductory promotion

introductory_share.unit: approximate percent of purchase volume and outstanding balances on introductory promotional-rate cards

observations.method: CFPB analysis of issuer and credit-record data, reported by credit-score tier and promotional-rate product.
observations.uncertainty: The report states that purchase volume and balance measures have different universes and that promotional rates temporarily reduce revolving-credit cost; later balances can be higher for promotional accounts. The tier comparison is not a causal treatment effect.
observations.subgroup: Prime-plus and lower-score cardholders; cards with zero-percent introductory APR promotions versus other cards.
observations.counterinterpretation: Prime-plus growth may reflect account mix, credit access, or spending capacity rather than a reward-driven transfer; promotional borrowing can smooth a shock or defer a larger future balance.

denominator.unit: US dollars in disputed credit-card charges

recurring_transaction_share.unit: percent of disputes involving cancelled recurring transactions such as subscriptions, memberships, and utility bills

below_prime_balance_concentration.unit: percent of below-prime balances held by issuers with less than $100 billion in assets

observations.method: CFPB report analysis of issuer/credit-record and transaction-dispute data; dispute categories are administrative market measures.
observations.uncertainty: A dispute is not equivalent to an erroneous charge, successful refund, or verified consumer harm. The below-prime issuer concentration is a balance distribution, not a measure of approval, price, or remedy quality.
observations.subgroup: Cardholders with below-prime credit scores and consumers disputing recurring transactions; issuer-size categories.
observations.counterinterpretation: Recurring-transaction disputes may reflect ordinary cancellation friction, merchant billing systems, or consumer confusion; the report does not make this share a measure of platform wrongdoing or household loss.

boundary: This record describes CFPB market, account, credit-tier, and dispute measures as of 2024. It does not establish a same-household burden, causal effect of rewards or APRs, successful dispute remedy, or the size of the NBER-modeled merchant transfer. Market totals, balances, fees, and disputed charges retain separate universes and meanings.
